title: Man. Post. Cap. II §III: Placeus — analogy opposite; passive justice omitted; false consensus
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. This like thing is not juxtaposed, but opposite. For to this bland prestidigitator I am as dissimilar as white to black. First he would pretend to have enumerated all acceptations of Christ's justice, when yet he would omit one in the business of justification most momentous, by which Christ's justice is taken for that singular obedience which he rendered by suffering death, death, I say, of the cross; which is commonly called passive justice, and is believed without doubt by all Protestants to be imputed to the faithful, when concerning the imputation of active justice, which alone D. Gar. commemorated, there is some discrepancy of opinions, which does not disturb the Church's peace. But I reviewed all acceptations of Adam's first sin, I omitted none. Second he would say that Christ's justice taken in that sense is imputed, in which sense taken it is constantly denied to be imputed by all Protestants. But I affirmed that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity in that sense in which all Protestants constantly hold it is imputed to them. Therefore he would feign a consensus with the Evangelicals plainly false: For who ever of the Evangelicals taught that the inhering justice which we have from Christ is imputed to us unto justification? But the consensus which I profess is true, and is not denied, nor can be denied by anyone not Pelagian.
pass_b_english: Placeus. This likeness is not a parallel but an opposite. To that bland prestidigitator I am as unlike as white to black. First, he would pretend to have listed every sense of Christ's righteousness, yet omit the one most decisive in justification: that singular obedience he rendered by suffering death—death, I say, of the cross—which is commonly called passive righteousness and which all Protestants without hesitation believe is imputed to believers, while about imputing active righteousness (the only sense D. Garissoles mentioned) there is some difference of opinion that does not disturb the Church's peace. I, by contrast, reviewed every sense of Adam's first sin and omitted none. Second, he would say that Christ's righteousness, taken in a sense in which all Protestants constantly deny it is imputed, is imputed; whereas I affirmed that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity in the sense in which all Protestants constantly hold it is. So he would invent a plainly false consensus with the Evangelicals: for who among them ever taught that the inhering righteousness we have from Christ is imputed to us for justification? The consensus I profess is true, and no one who is not a Pelagian denies it or can deny it.
source_text: PLAC. Hoc simile non est appositum, sed oppositum. Huic enim blandulo praestigiatori tam sum dissimilis quam album nigro. Primo ille se enumerasse prae se ferret omnes acceptiones justitiae Christi, cum tamen unam omitteret in justificationis negotio maxime momentosam, qua justitia Christi accipitur pro singulari illa obedientia quam praestitit patiendo mortem, mortem, inquam, crucis; quae vulgo justitia passiva appellatur, et imputari fidelibus ab omnibus Protestantibus sine dubitatione creditur, cum de imputatione justitiae activae, quam solam D. Gar. commemoravit, sit aliqua sententiarum discrepantia, quae pacem Ecclesiae non turbat. Ego vero primi Adae peccati acceptiones omnes recensui, nullam praetermisi. Secundo ille Christi justitiam eo sensu acceptam imputari diceret, quo sensu accepta imputari negatur constanter ab omnibus Protestantibus. Ego vero peccatum Adami eo sensu posteris imputari affirmavi, quo sensu iis imputari omnes Protestantes constanter tenent. Itaque ille consensum fingeret cum Evangelicis plane falsum: Quis enim unquam Evangelicorum docuit justitiam inhaerentem, quam habemus a Christo, nobis ad justificationem imputari? Quem autem ego profiteor consensum, is verus est, neque negatur, aut negari potest a quoquam non Pelagiano.

choices.choice: Analogy opposite; omitted passiva; Placeus consensus true not feigned

notes: Cap. II §III Garissoles densify section 169 from locked 1661 Latin (pp. 165 tip–170 tip).
